hook.text: A language model never sees your text. It's cut into tokens, tokens become vectors, and attention lets every vector look at every other. Each step is a choice with a cost, and this round asks you to defend it.

plan.text: Nineteen questions: fourteen worked through, and five quickly at the end.

q1.text: Question one. What is tokenization, and why is subword tokenization standard?

q1-a.text: It splits text into the units a model reads, and every choice of unit trades vocabulary against length.

q1-word.text: Whole words need a vast vocabulary and still miss new ones. Build one from this track's seven other pages, three thousand words, and read the NLP page with it: fifteen percent of its words were never seen, hallucination among them, and each becomes the same unknown token.

q1-char.text: Characters never miss, but they make the page five times as long as subword tokens do, and attention's cost grows with the square: twenty-five times.

q1-sub.text: Subwords split the difference: frequent words stay whole, and rare ones break into known pieces.

q1-cost.text: The vocabulary has a price too: each piece is a row of the embedding table, so at a width of four thousand and ninety-six, that's over eight hundred million weights.

emb-in.text: What goes in those rows is the next question.

q2.text: Question two. What are word embeddings? Contrast word2vec and GloVe.
q2.spoken: Question two. What are word embeddings? Contrast word2vec and glove.

q2-a.text: An embedding is a learned, dense vector for something discrete, a word, a user, a product, placed so that similar things land near each other. In a model, it's a lookup table with one row per id.

q2-how.text: word2vec learns word vectors by prediction: a shallow network, given a word, predicts its neighbors. GloVe counts how often words occur together across the whole corpus, and factorizes that table. Both give each word one fixed vector.
q2-how.spoken: word2vec learns word vectors by prediction: a shallow network, given a word, predicts its neighbors. Glove counts how often words occur together across the whole corpus, and factorizes that table. Both give each word one fixed vector.

q3.text: Question three. What is the difference between static and contextual embeddings?

q3-a.text: A static vector puts bank at one point, river or money. A transformer computes a fresh vector for each occurrence from the words around it, so the two banks separate. That's a big reason transformers won.

q3-cost.text: The price: a contextual vector costs a pass through the model, where a static one is a table lookup.

attn-in.text: The mechanism behind that is attention.

q4-a.text: Each token is projected into a query, a key and a value. One token's weight on another is its query dotted with the other's key, divided by the square root of the key's dimension, and softmaxed. Its output is the weighted sum of the values.

q4-scale.text: Why divide? Simulate queries and keys of sixty-four random numbers: their dot products spread eight times wider than the numbers do, and softmax puts on average eighty-five percent of a row's weight on one key, where its gradient is small. Divided by eight, the square root of sixty-four, the top weight averages twenty-five percent.

q4-hop.text: Every pair of tokens is one hop apart, so distance costs nothing, but the pairs grow with the square of the length.

q5.text: Question five. What is multi-head attention, and why use it?

q5-a.text: Give each head its own smaller query, key and value, run attention in each, in parallel, and concatenate the results. One head can track syntax, another which noun a pronoun means.

q5-cost.text: And eight heads of sixty-four cost the same multiply-adds as one head of five hundred and twelve.

q6.text: Question six. Describe the transformer architecture.

q6-a.text: A stack of blocks: multi-head self-attention, then a feed-forward network at each position, each wrapped in a residual connection and layer norm. Attention ignores order, so positional encodings add it.

q6-kinds.text: Encoder-only models like BERT attend both ways, for understanding. Decoder-only models like GPT mask the future, for generation. Encoder-decoder models like T5 turn one sequence into another.
q6-kinds.spoken: Encoder-only models like bert attend both ways, for understanding. Decoder-only models like GPT mask the future, for generation. Encoder-decoder models like T5 turn one sequence into another.

q7.text: Question seven. Why did transformers replace RNNs for most NLP?

q7-a.text: An RNN squeezes everything through one hidden state, one step at a time: slow to train, and forgetful over distance.

cost-in.text: The trade-off is attention's own cost.

q8.text: Question eight. Why is attention's cost a scaling bottleneck for long documents?

q8-a.text: Every token is compared with every other. A thousand tokens make a million pairs; two thousand, four million. Double the context, and attention costs about four times as much.

q8-when.text: The rest of a layer only grows linearly, though. For a model four thousand and ninety-six wide, with the usual feed-forward four times that, attention's arithmetic outweighs the rest only past about twenty-five thousand tokens.

q8-fix.text: Past that, teams reach for sparse, sliding-window or linear attention, or retrieve the passages that matter instead of pasting in everything.

q9.text: Question nine. What is a context window, and why does its size matter?

q9-a.text: It's the most tokens, prompt and output together, that the model can attend to at once. Instructions, documents and history all compete for it, a longer one costs more, and anything past the limit is invisible.

train-in.text: So much for the shape. Next, how it learns.

q10.text: Question ten. What is pretraining, and what objectives are used?

q10-a.text: Training on a huge unlabeled corpus, where the text is its own label. Masked language modeling, BERT's, hides tokens and predicts them from both sides. Causal language modeling, GPT's, predicts the next token from the left alone, which is what lets it generate.
q10-a.spoken: Training on a huge unlabeled corpus, where the text is its own label. Masked language modeling, bert's, hides tokens and predicts them from both sides. Causal language modeling, GPT's, predicts the next token from the left alone, which is what lets it generate.

q11.text: Question eleven. What is the difference between pretraining and fine-tuning?

q11-a.text: Pretraining is the expensive phase, once per model. Fine-tuning cheaply adapts it to one task, on a much smaller labeled set. Instruction tuning and RLHF, reinforcement learning from human feedback, then teach it to follow instructions and match human preferences.

lora-in.text: Even fine-tuning can be made far cheaper.

q12.text: Question twelve. What is parameter-efficient fine-tuning, for example LoRA?
q12.spoken: Question twelve. What is parameter-efficient fine-tuning, for example laura?

q12-a.text: LoRA, low-rank adaptation, freezes the model and learns an update to some of its matrices, as the product of two thin ones.
q12-a.spoken: Laura, low-rank adaptation, freezes the model and learns an update to some of its matrices, as the product of two thin ones.

q12-math.text: A matrix four thousand and ninety-six square holds nearly seventeen million numbers. At rank eight, the two thin ones hold sixty-five thousand: under half a percent.

q12-ship.text: Adapt two matrices in each of thirty-two layers, and you train about four million weights out of six and a half billion, and ship an eight-megabyte adapter instead of a thirteen-gigabyte copy.

q12-serve.text: At serving, merge it into the weights and it adds no latency, or keep it separate, and one base model serves many adapters.

rag-in.text: Fine-tuning changes how a model behaves. What it knows is another matter.

q13.text: Question thirteen. What is retrieval-augmented generation, RAG, and why use it?

q13-a.text: Embed the query, fetch the most similar passages from a vector store, and put them in the prompt for the model to answer from. It grounds answers, adds fresh or private knowledge without retraining, and lets you cite sources.

q13-miss.text: But the answer is only as good as the retrieval. Search this track's hundred and sixty-seven answers by shared words for how to stop an LLM making things up: the hallucination answer scores zero, sharing none of those words. Retrieval has to match meaning, which is what embeddings are for, usually alongside keyword search for exact names.

q14.text: Question fourteen. When would you choose RAG over fine-tuning, and vice versa?

q14-a.text: RAG for knowledge: facts that change, are private, or are too many to memorize, since updating the store needs no training. Fine-tuning for behavior: a style, a vocabulary, an output format. They compose: fine-tune for behavior, retrieve for facts.

q14-cost.text: And count the bill: RAG pays on every request, in retrieval time and prompt tokens, while fine-tuning pays up front, and again each time it's retrained.

r-beyond.text: Embeddings beyond the input: encode documents, products or users once, then find neighbors by cosine similarity, for search, clustering, deduplication and recommendations, with no labels.

r-halluc.text: Hallucination: a model is trained to write probable text, not true text, so it invents fluently, most of all on niche facts. Ground it with retrieval and citations, lower the temperature for facts, add checks, and keep a human in the loop where stakes are high. Nothing removes it entirely.

r-prompt.text: Prompting steers a frozen model with text alone.

r-random.text: Randomness: temperature divides the scores before the softmax, so near zero is almost greedy, and higher is more varied. Top-k keeps the k likeliest tokens; top-p, the smallest set whose probabilities add up past p. Keep it low for extraction, higher for brainstorming.

r-eval.text: And evaluation depends on the task: perplexity for language modeling, BLEU for translation, ROUGE for summaries, exact match and F1 for extracted answers. Overlap misses meaning, so teams add human ratings and LLM judges, on a held-out set that looks like real use.
r-eval.spoken: And evaluation depends on the task: perplexity for language modeling, blue for translation, rooj for summaries, exact match and F1 for extracted answers. Overlap misses meaning, so teams add human ratings and LLM judges, on a held-out set that looks like real use.

next.text: But a model in a notebook isn't a product yet. Next: ML system design, the system around it.

r-prompt-cheap.text: It's the cheapest lever, so try it before fine-tuning.

q1-piece.text: A production tokenizer with two hundred thousand pieces splits the word hallucination in two, and averages one point four tokens a word on this page.

q6-modern.text: Today's LLMs keep that skeleton, with three changes: the norm before each sub-layer, rotary embeddings for relative position, and a gated activation instead of ReLU.

q9-rag.text: A window big enough for every document still doesn't retire retrieval: every prompt token is paid for on every request, and answers tend to get worse as loosely relevant text fills it.

r-prompt-kinds.text: Zero-shot describes the task, few-shot adds worked examples, and chain-of-thought asks for step-by-step reasoning, which helps on multi-step problems, though a model that already reasons gains little from it but tokens and latency.

q7-tf.text: A transformer links any two tokens directly and, in training, processes every position at once, which is what a GPU is built for.

q1-bpe.text: Those pieces come from byte-pair encoding: start from single bytes, and keep merging the most frequent adjacent pair until the vocabulary is full.

q7-grad.text: Its gradients shrink with every step back, so distant words barely count.

r-random-host.text: A hosted reasoning model may refuse these settings; there, you steer with the prompt, a reasoning-effort setting and structured outputs.
